fetched_contents.text: Chemical Composition, Biological Activity, and Potential Uses of Oregano (Origanum vulgare L.) and Oregano Essential Oil Abstract Medicinal aromatic plants (MAPs) are a rich and diverse source of traditional and modern medicines. Aromatic plants contain valuable essential oils that exhibit numerous biological activities. Essential oils are used in pharmaceutical production, cosmetics, and food preservation to ensure the microbiological stability of products. Plants from the Lamiaceae family, including Origanum vulgare L., are a source of raw materials with antimicrobial and antioxidant properties, and they can be utilized in the production of new drugs and other bioproducts. Oregano is an example of a plant with great potential, known for its traditional health-related and culinary applications and its growing significance in the production of medicines, cosmetics, antiseptics, and preservatives. This work aims to consolidate the current research results on the occurrence, acquisition, use, and medicinal and dietary value of common oregano and oregano essential oil. The obtained results indicate that oregano is a valuable medicinal and culinary plant, serving as a source of natural antiseptics and protective agents. Oregano essential oil, rich in thymol and carvacrol, has a number of health-promoting properties. These compounds (also present in extracts) exhibit significant antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antiangiogenic, anticancer, and antimicrobial activities. The research findings highlight the promising role of these compounds as potential structures in the search for new antimicrobial and antibiofilm agents. Keywords: Lamiaceae, medicinal and aromatic plants, natural antibacterial agents, antioxidant activity 1. Introduction Medicinal aromatic plants (MAPs) are a rich and diverse source of traditional and modern medicines and cosmetics. Among them are wild plants and plants grown in herbal plantations, known for their traditional medicinal and culinary uses and processing. The unique aroma of MAPs is associated with the presence of essential oils (EOs), volatile substances of a complex chemical nature [1]. EOs contain terpene compounds, such as alcohol derivatives (geraniol, α-bisabolol), ketones (menthone, p-vetivone), aldehydes (citronellal, sinensal), esters (γ-terpinyl acetate, cedryl acetate), and phenols (thymol), as well as non-terpene compounds and aromatic phenylpropane derivatives, including eugenol, cinnamaldehyde, and safrole. The primary metabolic precursors of terpenoids and phenylpropanoids are compounds produced by various biosynthetic pathways/routes [2]. EOs are secondary metabolites, plant secretions that can perform essential functions in the plant body: they can protect against viruses, bacteria, fungi, insects, and herbivores, as well as attract potential pollinators [3]. The biological properties of EOs are generally associated with their significant constituents, which are present at 20–70% [4]. EOs are used in pharmaceutical production, cosmetics, and food preservation to ensure the microbiological stability of products. In aromatherapy, their valuable therapeutic properties are utilized, including their antiinflammatory, antimicrobial, antioxidant, sedative, analgesic, and antistress properties [5]. In addition to EOs, other bioactive components of MAPs, including active polyphenols [1,6,7], also have potential applications in medicine and pharmacy. The Lamiaceae family includes many MAP species valued for their use in medicine, food, and cosmetics. It is one of the most essential plant groups producing EOs with antioxidant and antimicrobial properties. Lamiaceae plants have been proven to be a source of raw material with antimalarial [8], antimicrobial [9], and antioxidant [10] properties and can be used in the production of new drugs and other bioproducts such as flavorings, cosmetics, or preservatives [11]. One of the better-known members of the Lamiaceae family is the genus Origanum, which includes Mediterranean plant species traditionally used as spices and medicines. 2. Materials and Methods Scientific information was obtained by searching the resources of available databases (CABI, EBSCO, Science Direct, Find Articles, JCR, Medline, Oxford Journals, Scopus, Springer, Web of Science, Wiley) to review and consolidate the results of current research on the occurrence, acquisition, use, and dietary and medicinal value of common oregano (Origanum vulgare L., Lamiaceae) plants. A classical methodology consisting of keyword generation, systematic search, cataloguing, and subsequent discussion of relevant scientific information was used. The conclusion summarizes recent critical literature data and outlines further research perspectives. 3. Results 3.1. Species Description, Occurrence, Traditional Use The genus Origanum (Lamiaceae) is divided into ten sections comprising 43 species, 6 subspecies, 3 cultivars, and 18 natural hybrids, including annuals, perennials, and shrubs, which are commonly found in the Mediterranean, Euro–Siberian, and Iranian–Siberian regions [12]. Most species in the genus (about 75%) are found in the western Mediterranean area, with 16 considered endemic to Turkey [13]. Wild oregano species are found at different altitudes, from coastal to mountainous areas, on different soils, have high light requirements, and can withstand relatively low temperatures. The more important genera of oregano include Greek oregano (O. vulgare L. ssp. hirtum), Turkish oregano (O. onites L.), common oregano (O. vulgare L. ssp. vulgare), and O. vulgare L. ssp. viridulum [14]. Essential Oil Abstract Due to the plethora of pharmacological activities reported in the literature, Origanum vulgare L. is a valuable aromatic plant for the medicine of the XXI century. Recent studies highlight that Origanum vulgare L. essential oil (OvEo) has gained attention in the dermatological field due to the cosmeceutical potential correlated with the presence of thymol and carvacrol. As a result of the fulminant expansion of bacterial resistance to antibiotics and the aggressiveness of skin infections, OvEo was extensively studied for its antimicrobial activity against Staphyloccocus spp. and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Moreover, researchers have also assessed the anti-inflammatory activity of OvEo, suggesting its tissue remodeling and wound healing potential. Whereas OvEo comprises important biological activities that are used in a wide range of pathologies, recently, essential oils have shown great potential in the development of new therapeutic alternatives for skin disorders, such as acne, wounds or aging. Furthermore, substantial efforts have been committed to the development of modern formulations, such as microemulsions and nanoemulsions, in order to create the possibility for topical application. The review brings to the fore the most recent findings in the dermatological field regarding potential plant-based therapies involving OvEo, emphasizing the modern pharmaceutical formulation approaches and the cutaneous benefits in skin disorders. Introduction Currently, the use of medicinal plants in the form of various extracts (total, concentrated or standardized) and in the form of isolated pure phytocompounds for therapeutic purposes for acute and/or chronic pathologies, as well as for prevention, plays an important role in modern medicine. Thus, in recent decades, the development of phytotherapy has undergone an impressive evolution, especially in the design and implementation of new therapeutic strategies [1]. At present, many of the drugs currently used in therapeutic protocols are obtained from medicinal plants. Moreover, chemical synthetized molecules often have natural molecules as a starting point [2]. It is well known that nowadays the industry is still in full development; furthermore, it is faced with important problems, such as the depletion of resources, as well as waste and pollutant production in large quantities [3]. Attempts are being made to find perspectives such as the use of renewable natural resources accompanied by technologies that lead to a dispersion of pollutants in a smaller amount into the atmosphere and waste management [3,4]. Although chemical synthesis is quite widely used from an industrial point of view, considerable and viable alternatives have been found, such as the development of biotechnology and the use of natural compounds in many fields of activity [4,5,6]. From antiquity to present, essential oils have been one of the most commonly employed natural products. Essential oils (EOs) are natural, complex, liquid and volatile compounds obtained as products of secondary metabolism from aromatic plants. They are usually characterized by a strong odor and can be extracted from different vegetal products of aromatic plants, such as roots, wood, leaves, flowers, fruits and whole plants [7]. It is also important to acknowledge that the production of EOs depends on certain factors, including (i) the method of extraction, (ii) drying and storage, (iii) harvesting time, (iv) climatic conditions, (v) crop location, (vi) types of plant species and (vii) the part of the plant employed [7,8,9]. Obtaining EOs, concentration and purification can be performed via different physico-chemical methods, such as (i) pressing, (ii) distillation (hydro-distillation or steam entrainment) and (iii) extraction (solvent extraction, microwave or ultrasound-assisted extraction) [7,9,10]. The choice of a suitable method for obtaining EOs will depend on the final applicability of the obtained extracts. Volatile oils are widely used all over the world and have numerous applications in multiple industries, such as the pharmaceutical, cosmetics, food and perfume industries [7,11]. As a result of the complexity of active compounds, EOs also have a number of disadvantages, such as high volatility, poor solubility in water and thermal and chemical labilities to the action of exogenous agents [7,12]. Thus, for the pharmaceutic and cosmetic industry, the use of EOs in formulations requires the rigorous control of their conditioning and storage conditions [7]. Indeed, due to the complexity of the active compounds, fragrant properties and a plethora of biological effects, EOs can be considered as a resource of natural therapeutic ingredients that can be used in the formulation of a broad range of cosmetic products (creams, emulsions, conditioners, hair repairing shampoos and lotions) [13,14]. Moreover, it is important to avoid their direct application onto the skin because they can induce the occurrence of serious side effects (irritation, darkening of the skin and allergic contact dermatitis) [15,16,17]. fetched_contents.text: Oregano Oil Side Effects: What You Should Know Unlike the herb you cook with, commercially-prepared oregano oil is highly concentrated and should be diluted before use. Side effects can include nausea and vomiting. Oregano essential oil is made from the leaves of the oregano plant. Even though oregano is a well-known herb found in many kitchens, oregano herbal oils and oregano essential oils aren’t used for cooking. Rather, the essential oil is used both topically and through inhalation to treat specific health conditions. The herbal oil can be taken as an herbal supplement. Read on to learn more about its forms, uses, side effects, and when to contact a doctor. While research suggests there are health benefits, the FDA doesn’t monitor or regulate the purity or quality of essential oils. It’s important to talk with a healthcare professional before you begin using essential oils and be sure to research the quality of a brand’s products. Always do a patch test before trying a new essential oil. Forms Oregano oil extract is an herbal supplement. It’s available in supplement form, as a pill, and as a softgel capsule. These usually contain other ingredients to dilute oregano oil, since it’s very potent. The capsules can be taken orally, or cut open and applied to the skin, provided they’re not full strength. Oregano oil is also available as a highly concentrated essential oil that comes in liquid form. The oil may come premixed with a carrier oil, or it may be purchased full strength. For topical use, if it’s not premixed, you’ll have to dilute it yourself by combining it with a carrier oil, such as coconut or olive oil. The usual recipe is 5 to 6 drops for every ounce of carrier oil. You don’t need to dilute essential oils for inhalation or use in a diffuser or vaporizer. The essential oil can be used topically after it’s diluted. Don’t take any essential oil orally without seeing a certified aromatherapist first. Some essential oils are toxic, and their qualities vary. Oregano essential oil can also be used in steam, as a vapor to be inhaled. This is done by putting one or two drops in a vaporizer or bowl of steaming water. Uses and benefits Oregano oil contains chemical compounds, including phenolic glycosides (phenols). These compounds have antioxidant and antimicrobial properties. Phenols, such as carvacrol, cymene, terpinine, and thymol, account for much of the composition of oregano oil. It’s the phenols in oregano oil that may make it beneficial. Oregano essential oil may be for: * digestion * mouth and throat rinses * inhalations * upper respiratory tract inflammation * medicinal baths While much of this research is promising, it’s by no means definitive proof that oregano oil is effective. Even so, this product is marketed for many uses. Potential uses: * improved mood * bacterial infections, such as E. coli * viruses, such as the norovirus (stomach virus) or upper respiratory infections * small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) * parasitic infections * urinary tract infections (UTIs) * yeast infections * acne * dandruff * eczema Side effects and risks Unlike the herb you cook with, commercially-prepared oregano oil is highly concentrated. It’s easy to take too much or to use it for too long. When used as directed, oregano oil should be safe. In too-high doses, it may have detrimental effects. This may be due in part to thymol, one of the phenols it contains. In high doses, thymol is a mild irritant that might affect the skin or internal organs. It can cause: * nausea * vomiting * gastric distress * central hyperactivity Thymol may also be irritating or corrosive to the skin and eyes. Oregano oil should never be applied to broken skin or used on or near the eyes. Oregano oil may cause an allergic reaction in some people. If you’re allergic to oregano or to other plants in the Lamiaceae family, such as mint, sage, basil, and lavender, don’t use oregano oil. When used topically, diluted oregano essential oil may cause a skin rash, even in people who aren’t allergic to it. It’s important to check with your doctor before using oregano oil and to follow package directions exactly, whether you’re using the capsules or essential oil. There’s been no medical research done on oregano oil’s safety for children, or for pregnant or breastfeeding women. These populations shouldn’t use oregano oil. Proper dosage and guidelines Medicinal dosages of oregano oil for people hasn’t been studied in-depth. Commercially-sold supplements and essential oils have recommended doses, established by their manufacturers. These take the amount of thymol and other phenols into account. It’s important not to exceed the recommended dosage given or to take oregano oil in any form, including on the skin, for more than several weeks. When using oregano essential oil, a little goes a very long way.One to two drops of diluted oil may not seem like much, but exceeding that dosage may cause adverse reactions to occur. When to contact your doctor Symptoms of oregano allergy can include rash, stomach distress, or trouble breathing. It’s especially important not to inhale oregano oil if you might be allergic to it. Doing so can cause inflammation of the airways and might quickly become dangerous. Takeaway There are many claims about oregano oil’s ability to soothe symptoms and cure medical conditions. However, there’s very little evidence to back up these claims. If you decide to take oregano oil, either as a supplement or essential oil, make sure to follow dosage directions exactly and check with your doctor before use. Remember that essential oils are much stronger than the supplements and should always be diluted. Oregano oils shouldn’t be used in babies or children, or if you’re pregnant or nursing.

Mechanisms of therapeutic action relevant to skin treatment

The major constituents of Origanum vulgare essential oil reported in the evidence are carvacrol, thymol, and, in some formulations, linalool and other minor phenolic or terpene compounds. The evidence consistently identifies carvacrol and thymol as central bioactive components, with carvacrol especially emphasized as a primary therapeutic compound in the oil [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2]. The pharmacological profile described for carvacrol includes antimicrobial, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer, immunomodulatory, hepatoprotective, and anti-adipogenic activities, while thymol is similarly described as a major compound with potent anthelmintic, fungicidal, and other bioactive properties [N2-R4][N2-R5][N2-F2]. This dual emphasis on carvacrol and thymol suggests that their antimicrobial and antifungal activity is a core mechanism of action relevant to skin treatment.

For antimicrobial and antifungal activity, the evidence is directly supportive. Carvacrol is repeatedly described as having potent antimicrobial and antifungal properties, while thymol is noted as fungicidal and as a major bioactive compound in the oil [N2-R4][N2-R5][N2-F2]. The broader literature on O. vulgare also positions thymol and carvacrol as the main volatiles in oregano EOs and as compounds with broad biological activities, including antimicrobial action [N2-F2]. This makes the oil biologically attractive for skin conditions involving bacterial or fungal infection, where microbial clearance is a therapeutic goal.

The evidence also supports anti-inflammatory pathways and skin barrier effects. Carvacrol is described as having anti-inflammatory activity, and the review on O. vulgare notes that thymol and carvacrol are associated with anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antiangiogenic, anticancer, and antimicrobial activities [N2-F2]. In the skin-related evidence, antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties are directly linked to wound healing and skin protection. The review on cutaneous benefits of O. vulgare notes that the oil has been studied for anti-inflammatory activity and tissue remodeling potential, which are relevant to skin barrier repair and inflammation reduction [N4-F3]. A separate source on essential oils and wound healing also states that essential oils help prevent infection due to their antibacterial and anti-inflammatory effects [N3-R4]. This indicates that the major constituents contribute to skin treatment not only through direct microbial suppression but also through modulation of inflammatory responses.

Potential antioxidant and wound-healing properties are also supported by the evidence. Carvacrol is explicitly described as having antioxidant activity, and thymol and carvacrol together are presented as compounds with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial activities [N2-R5][N2-F2]. The review on O. vulgare further states that OvEo has gained attention in the dermatological field due to its antimicrobial activity against Staphylococcus spp. and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, anti-inflammatory activity, and tissue remodeling and wound-healing potential [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that OvEo is studied for its cutaneous benefits in skin disorders such as acne, wounds, or aging [N4-F3]. This makes antioxidant and wound-healing effects plausible therapeutic pathways for topical application.

Overall, the evidence points to a mechanism in which carvacrol and thymol act as the major antimicrobial and antifungal agents, while also contributing anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and tissue-remodeling effects that support skin barrier function and wound healing [N2-R4][N2-R5][N2-F2][N4-F3]. The skin-related evidence further supports these mechanisms by associating antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties with wound healing and skin protection [N3-R4][N4-F3]. A limitation of the evidence provided here is that the cited materials are mostly reviews and mechanistic summaries rather than direct mechanistic studies, so the pathways are inferred from compound activity rather than experimentally resolved in detail [N2-F2][N4-F3].
node_outputs.N10:
Evidence base for skin-related applications

The evidence base for skin-related applications of Origanum vulgare is mixed but suggestive, with a stronger emphasis on in vitro and formulation studies than on clinical trials. The most direct evidence cited here is that OvEo has been studied for antimicrobial activity against Staphylococcus spp. and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and for anti-inflammatory activity and tissue remodeling potential, which are linked to wound-healing potential [N4-F3]. The review also notes that OvEo has been explored for its cutaneous benefits in skin disorders such as acne, wounds, or aging, and that modern formulations such as microemulsions and nanoemulsions have been developed to enable topical application [N4-F3]. This indicates a research trajectory from biological activity to practical topical delivery.

For acne, the evidence is specific and direct. One source reports that oregano EO was formulated as a nanoemulsion because of in vitro antibacterial results against acne-causing bacteria, and another study explicitly assessed the potential anti-acne activity of selected EOs commonly used in Mediterranean folk medicine [N4-R2][N4-R3]. These sources support a direct evidence base for anti-acne application, but they are in vitro or formulation-based rather than clinical. The review on cutaneous benefits also notes that OvEo has been assessed for anti-acne activity, reinforcing the relevance of the compound profile to acne treatment [N4-F3].

For wound healing, the evidence is similarly supportive. The review states that OvEo has been studied for anti-inflammatory activity and tissue remodeling and wound-healing potential [N4-F3]. Additional skin-related evidence on essential oils reports that antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory effects help prevent infection and support wound healing, and another source notes that topical application of Cinnamon verum essential oil accelerates infected wound healing by increasing tissue antioxidant capacity and keratin [N3-R4][N3-R5]. While the latter is not OvEo, it is chemically and mechanistically relevant and shows that skin-healing literature often frames essential oils as wound-promoting agents. The evidence also mentions that wound-healing studies have used hydrogels and polymer-based scaffolds incorporating selected essential oils, suggesting that topical delivery formats are part of the research strategy [N3-R1][N3-R3]. This indicates that wound-healing evidence exists, but it is often in vitro or in vivo in small animal models rather than large-scale human clinical trials.

For eczema and fungal infections, the evidence is less direct. The review on cutaneous benefits notes anti-inflammatory activity and anti-acne activity, but it does not explicitly cite eczema evidence [N4-F3]. The skin-related evidence does note antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties relevant to infected wounds, but eczema-specific evidence is not clearly established in the provided materials [N3-R4][N4-F3]. The evidence provided here also does not include strong clinical studies on OvEo for eczema, so this remains a gap. For fungal infections, the evidence is indirectly supportive because carvacrol and thymol are described as having fungicidal activity [N2-R4][N2-F2], but the provided materials do not include a direct clinical or in vitro study of OvEo specifically against fungi relevant to skin infections.

Strength of evidence is therefore uneven. In vitro and formulation studies are abundant, especially for acne and wound healing, while clinical evidence is sparse. The review on cutaneous benefits emphasizes that OvEo is being studied for acne, wounds, or aging, and that modern formulations have been developed to enable topical use, but it also notes that the evidence is by no means definitive [N4-F3]. The nanoemulsion study cited as evidence is a formulation study, not a clinical trial [N4-R2]. The same is true of the in vitro study on acne-causing bacteria [N4-R3]. This means the evidence base is strong for biological plausibility and formulation development, but weak for large-scale clinical proof.

Limitations and gaps include a lack of robust clinical trials, limited direct evidence for eczema, and the fact that many studies are in vitro or in vivo in animal models. Another gap is that the provided materials do not clearly establish long-term safety or repeated-dose effects for topical use in skin conditions, which is important for practical translation [N4-F3]. In short, the evidence supports acne and wound-healing relevance, but the evidence base for eczema and fungal infections is thin, and clinical translation remains limited [N4-F3][N3-R4].

Core chemical constituents and their relative abundance

The core chemical constituents of Origanum vulgare essential oil are most commonly identified as carvacrol, thymol, and other phenolic and terpene compounds. The evidence from the oregano essential oil studies explicitly states that more than 50% of oregano oil consists of phenolic compounds, primarily carvacrol and thymol [N1-R2]. Another source notes that carvacrol is considered the predominant compound, followed by thymol (an isomer of carvacrol), p-cymene, and γ-terpinene [N1-R3]. A separate source also reports that the main constituents of oregano essential oil are carvacrol, thymol, linalool, p-cymene, and γ-terpinene [N1-R4]. The most detailed chemical composition study in the provided evidence identifies carvacrol and thymol as the main components, with specific leaf-flower oils containing 30.73% carvacrol and 18.81% thymol, plus p-cymene at 10.88% and other components totaling 72.21% [N1-F1]. This establishes carvacrol and thymol as the most abundant constituents, with p-cymene and γ-terpinene also present in significant quantities.

Relative concentrations across different chemotypes or plant parts are supported by the evidence, though the provided material is not exhaustive. Practical considerations for use in skin treatment

Dilution and safety concerns for topical application are the most clearly supported practical considerations in the evidence. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that commercially-prepared oregano oil is highly concentrated and should be diluted before use [N5-F4]. It also warns that oregano oil should never be applied to broken skin or near the eyes [N5-F4]. The safety source notes that oregano oil may cause an allergic reaction in some people, and that it may cause skin rash, even in people not allergic to it [N5-F4]. It also notes that thymol is a mild irritant that may affect the skin or internal organs, and that high doses may cause nausea, vomiting, gastric distress, and central hyperactivity [N5-F4]. This means that topical use is safest when diluted, and the evidence supports caution against direct application to intact skin, broken skin, or sensitive areas.

Formulation recommendations and delivery methods are also clearly addressed. The evidence recommends diluting oregano essential oil with a carrier oil, such as olive oil, and gives a typical dilution ratio of 5 to 6 drops per ounce of carrier oil [N5-F4]. These recommendations support the use of carrier oils to reduce toxicity and increase absorption [N5-F4]. The evidence also mentions that oregano oil is sometimes premixed with a carrier oil and that, if not premixed, it must be diluted by the user [N5-F4]. This indicates that formulation should prioritize dilution and carrier oil use rather than relying on undiluted essential oil.

Delivery methods are therefore best understood as carrier-oil-based dilution, with the oil applied topically after dilution. The evidence does not describe a wide range of delivery formats beyond carrier oils, but it does imply that dilution is the primary practical delivery strategy [N5-F4]. The safety source also notes that oregano oil can be used in steam or vaporized for inhalation, but this is not relevant to topical skin treatment [N5-F4]. For topical skin treatment, the evidence clearly supports dilution with carrier oil as the recommended approach [N5-F4][N5-R4].

Potential interactions or adverse effects are also well covered. The evidence notes that oregano oil may cause allergic reactions, skin rash, and irritation, and that thymol can be irritating or corrosive to the skin and eyes [N5-F4]. Adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, gastric distress, and central hyperactivity at high doses [N5-F4]. The evidence further notes that oregano oil should not be used by children, pregnant or breastfeeding women, or on broken skin, and that safety has not been established in these populations [N5-F4]. This means that use should be restricted to adults, with caution and medical consultation, especially for sensitive populations.

Overall, the practical considerations for skin treatment are clear: oregano oil must be diluted with a carrier oil, should not be used on broken skin or near the eyes, and should be used with caution due to potential irritation, allergic reactions, and toxicity at high doses [N5-F4][N5-R4]. The evidence notes that oregano oil may cause allergic reactions, skin rash, and irritation, and that thymol can be irritating or corrosive to the skin and eyes [N5-F4]. It also notes that people allergic to oregano or to other Lamiaceae family plants should avoid it [N5-F4]. Adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, gastric distress, and central hyperactivity at high doses [N5-F4]. The evidence further notes that oregano oil should not be used by children, pregnant or breastfeeding women, or on broken skin, and that safety has not been established in these populations [N5-F4]. This means that use should be restricted to adults, with caution and medical consultation, especially for sensitive populations [N5-F4].

## 6) Translation into topical skin delivery and formulation feasibility

Translation into topical skin delivery is constrained by the inherent properties of essential oils. The evidence notes that essential oils are volatile, hydrophobic, and have poor water solubility, which limits their bioavailability and skin penetration [N4-F3]. It also states that EOs are difficult to use directly on the skin because they can induce serious side effects such as irritation, darkening of the skin, and allergic contact dermatitis [N4-F3]. These properties suggest that direct topical application may be inefficient and unsafe, which is why dilution and carrier oils are recommended [N4-F3][N5-F4].

### Recommended delivery formats

The best-supported delivery formats are:

- **Dilution with carrier oils**, such as olive or coconut oil [N5-F4][N5-R4].
- **Nanoemulsions**, which improve EO bioactivities and skin permeation [N7-R1][N7-R3].

The nanoemulsion evidence also notes that nanoemulsions can be developed using techniques such as emulsion phase inversion and that they offer potential direct delivery to the skin [N7-R2]. This indicates that nanoemulsions are a promising advanced delivery approach [N7-R1][N7-R3].

### Barriers to practical translation from in vitro to clinical skin use

The main barriers to practical translation are:

- **Inherent limitations of EOs**: volatility, poor solubility, and instability make direct topical use inefficient and unsafe [N4-F3].
- **Need for dilution**: strong evidence supports carrier-oil dilution as the safest and most practical delivery method [N5-F4].
- **Weak clinical evidence**: many studies are in vitro or in vivo in small animal models rather than large-scale clinical trials [N4-F3][N3-R4].
- **Safety concerns**: irritation, allergic reactions, and toxicity at high doses limit practical use [N5-F4].
- **Lack of repeated-dose and long-term safety evidence**: the evidence does not provide strong evidence for repeated-dose effects or long-term safety in clinical populations [N4-F3][N5-F4].

## 7) Overall conclusion

In summary, **Origanum vulgare essential oil is chemically defined by carvacrol and thymol as its primary constituents**, with p-cymene and γ-terpinene also present in significant amounts [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1]. These compounds contribute to skin treatment through **antimicrobial/antifungal, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and wound-healing mechanisms** [N2-R4][N2-R5][N2-F2][N4-F3]. The evidence supports acne and wound-healing relevance, but the evidence base for eczema and fungal infections is thinner, and clinical translation remains limited [N4-F3][N3-R4]. Practical use should always be diluted with a carrier oil, and nanoemulsions offer a promising advanced delivery format to improve skin penetration and reduce irritation [N5-F4][N7-R1][N7-R3]. However, translation from in vitro to clinical use is constrained by formulation challenges, safety concerns, and the need for stronger clinical evidence [N4-F3][N5-F4].

## 8) Bottom line

If you want a short version: **O. vulgare essential oil is mainly carvacrol and thymol, which give antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and wound-healing effects; the evidence is strongest for acne and wound healing, but clinical proof is still limited; use it diluted with carrier oil, and nanoemulsions are a better delivery option than undiluted oil** [N1-R2][N2-R5][N4-F3][N5-F4][N7-R1].
